title: Human Compatible
subtitle: Artificial Intelligence and the Problem of Control
pitch: The co-author of the main AI textbook says the standard way of building AI, giving machines fixed goals, is broken, and proposes machines that are humble about what we want.

chapters.g: Russell asks what happens if AI research succeeds at its stated goal. He argues the field never seriously asked, and that success could be the biggest event in human history.
What intelligence is, from evolution and the brain to the idea of a rational agent that acts to achieve its objectives.

chapters.t: How might AI progress in the future?
chapters.g: The breakthroughs still needed for human level AI, such as language understanding and cumulative learning, and why timelines are hard to call.
Near term harms: surveillance, persuasion, autonomous weapons, job loss and the erosion of trust.
The gorilla problem (gorillas' fate depends on us) and the King Midas problem (getting exactly what you asked for). Fixed objectives plus great power is a recipe for disaster.
Russell answers common dismissals: 'we can just switch it off', 'it is too far away', 'just don't give it goals', and more.
His three principles: the machine's only goal is to realise human preferences, it is uncertain about what those are, and it learns them from human behaviour.
How these principles could be made precise with assistance games and inverse reinforcement learning, and why an uncertain machine lets you switch it off.
Humans are many, inconsistent, sometimes nasty and change over time. Learning their preferences is not simple.
What a world with beneficial AI might look like, and the risk of humans becoming too dependent on machines.
Appendix A: a gentle introduction to search and planning in AI.
Appendix B: how AI systems represent and reason with knowledge.
Appendix C: probability and Bayesian reasoning in AI.
Appendix D: machine learning, including deep learning, explained simply.

ideas: The standard model of AI (optimise a fixed objective) is dangerous when machines get powerful.
Machines should be uncertain about human preferences.
An uncertain machine has a reason to let you switch it off.
Learn human preferences from behaviour, not from a hand written goal.

args.a: Uncertainty about our goals makes machines defer to us, including letting us switch them off.
args.c: Critics note that once the machine is confident it knows what we want, the incentive to defer shrinks, and human behaviour is a noisy guide to human preferences.

args.a: We can make AI provably beneficial.
args.c: Proofs depend on models of humans and the world that may not hold. Today's large language models are not built as assistance games.

questions: Russell says 'you can't fetch the coffee if you're dead' style reasoning applies to almost any goal. Do you agree?
Should an AI do what you say, what you want, or what is good for you?
How could a machine learn the preferences of eight billion people who disagree?

o: Getting exactly what you asked for, with terrible results
quiz.w: Midas asked for everything he touched to turn to gold and got it.

quiz.q: In Russell's approach, what is the machine uncertain about?
quiz.w: Uncertainty about what we want is the key to safe behaviour.

quiz.q: Why would an uncertain machine allow itself to be switched off?
o: It treats our attempt to switch it off as evidence it is doing something we do not want
It is too weak to resist
